Chapter 4: Mental Models and Better Decisions—Seeing the World More Clearly
Every day, we make decisions—some are huge, some feel small—without really noticing how our thinking is shaped by hidden assumptions and mental shortcuts. Most folks end up relying on the same handful of tools, rarely stopping to ask if there might be a better way. But here’s the thing: people who actually pause, who take the time to look at their own thinking and build a wider set of mental models, usually make better choices. They sidestep the traps that catch so many others.
Picture this: someone’s facing a tough decision at work. The pressure’s on, the stakes are high, and it’s tempting to just go with the first idea or follow what everyone else is doing. But what if you could step back for a second and ask, “What am I missing here? How would someone from a totally different field see this?” Suddenly, you open up a whole new set of options.
This habit—using mental models, or ways of understanding the world borrowed from different fields—doesn’t just come naturally. It takes real effort to learn from psychology, economics, engineering, and more, and then actually use those lessons when you’re making decisions. But over time, it gets easier. Your mind starts to look for the right tool for each problem, instead of just falling back on old habits.
Let me give you an example. There was this business opportunity that looked almost too good to be true. Most people would’ve jumped right in, caught up in the excitement and the promise of quick rewards. But someone with a well-stocked toolkit stopped and thought about it through the lens of probability. What were the actual chances of success? What risks were hiding under the surface? By thinking like a mathematician—not just a businessperson—they dodged a really costly mistake.
Or take another situation: a friend wrestling with a personal dilemma. The answer wasn’t obvious, and emotions were running high. Instead of immediately giving advice, the listener leaned on some lessons from psychology, helping their friend spot the cognitive biases that were clouding their judgment. By shining a light on those hidden influences, they helped their friend make a much more thoughtful choice.
Again and again, it’s clear—the best decisions come from seeing the world as it really is, not just as we want it to be. That means being honest about what we don’t know, questioning our own assumptions, and welcoming new perspectives. And yes, it means being willing to change our minds when new evidence pops up, even if it’s uncomfortable.
Most of us resist this kind of thinking—it’s just easier to stick with what we know, to steer clear of uncertainty. But those who make a habit of learning from lots of different fields, who keep adding new mental models to their toolkit, end up better prepared for whatever life throws their way.
And here’s the best part: this approach isn’t just for business or investing. It shows up in every part of life—relationships, health, your own personal growth. The more tools you’ve got, the more likely you are to find the right solution, dodge costly mistakes, and build a life that’s not just successful, but honestly, a lot more satisfying.
